To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of drug-eluting stents in a real world population is associated with lower rates of target vessel revascularization (TVR), and that the majority of patients with restenosis after DES implantation have a favourable clinical course.
the use of a bimodal statistical distribution for angiographic restenosis is a valid method for evaluating the performance of coronary stents.
the use of a bimodal distribution of a surrogate end point in the design of a clinical study is a valid approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel, non-invasive, in vivo imaging technique for the assessment of restenosis in stented arteries.
the development of novel, efficient and reliable methods of analysis of the data obtained by the application of the various imaging modalities to biological systems.
understanding how the brain processes information about the environment, how the brain is organised, and how it changes over time.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of surrogate end points can be justified if they are validated and are shown to be predictive of clinical outcomes.

the surrogate end points have been used in clinical trials and they have helped to improve the understanding of the pathophysiology of disease and have been useful to design and test new therapies.4 However, the validity of a surrogate end point is not absolute and the relationship between the surrogate and the clinical end points should be established in a specific clinical context.5 In this regard, the concept of bimodality of angiographic measures after stent implantation is an interesting one.
the surrogate end point should be a valid and reliable measure of the true end point.4 In the field of coronary stents, the most widely used surrogate end points are restenosis and thrombosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bimodal distribution of restenosis is a consequence of the complex interaction between the stent and the vessel, which is influenced by the vessel size and stent size, and the stent type.

we have demonstrated that a bimodal distribution exists for the angiographic measures of stenosis after drug eluting stent implantation and that this bimodal distribution is associated with the presence of a stent strut in the lumen.
there is an important place for surrogate end points in cardiovascular medicine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of angiographically measured restenosis after DES implantation is bimodal.
the use of a surrogate end point is a trade-off: a reduction in the number of events needed to be observed to achieve adequate power is gained at the expense of a loss of clinical relevance.
the distribution of angiography-derived measures of restenotic lesion length and severity are bimodal in nature.
